items.title: Fluid balance
items.intro: Mr Tan is two days after bowel surgery. Help me total today's fluids in and out, so the doctor can see his balance.

recap.title: Balance worked out
recap.subtitle: Fluids in, fluids out, and a net balance that updates as the day goes on.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How much fluid has Mr Tan taken in?
questions.explanation_after_check: intake holds iv + oral: 1000 + 500 = 1500 mL.
questions.takeaway: So: names hold numbers, and later lines reuse them.

code_note.title: Variables
code_note.text: A name followed by `=` stores a value so later lines can use it.

science_note.title: Fluid balance
science_note.text: After surgery, nurses chart every fluid in and out. A balance far from zero can mean dehydration or overload.

questions.scene_label: A fluid balance scale with Mr Tan's intake going on the IN pan.

options.feedback: Numbers add up; they only join like that when they are text.

options.label: intake
options.feedback: print() shows the value a name holds, not the name.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Total what came out
questions.explanation_after_check: Urine and drain fluid both leave the body, so they add: 900 + 150 = 1050 mL.
questions.takeaway: So: every output is added in.
questions.hint_before_check: Both are fluid leaving the body.

code_note.title: Arithmetic
code_note.text: Python has a symbol for each kind of maths.

science_note.title: Counting every output
science_note.text: Drains, vomit and urine all count as output. Missing one makes a patient look more overloaded than they are.

questions.scene_label: The scale with the OUT pan waiting for its total.

options.feedback: 900 − 150 is 750: it hides the drain fluid instead of counting it.
900 × 150 is 135000, not a volume.
That runs without an error: output = urine = drain sets both names to 150, so output is only the drain.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The chart says Mr Tan is dry. Fix the balance.
questions.explanation_after_check: Net balance is intake minus output: 1500 − 1050 = +450 mL. Mr Tan kept 450 mL; the chart had him 450 mL dry.
questions.takeaway: So: balance = in − out.
questions.next_bridge: add a drink he has later.
questions.hint_before_check: Which way round is a balance?

code_note.title: Order matters
code_note.text: Some operations give a different answer when you swap their sides.

science_note.title: Why the sign matters
science_note.text: A positive balance means fluid kept in the body; a negative one, fluid lost. A flipped sign can lead to giving fluids to an overloaded patient.

questions.scene_label: The scale tips the way the code says.

c.feedback: That adds them: 2550 mL is the total volume moved, not the balance.
That gives -2550: both signs flipped.

d.feedback: That flips the sign on screen only; net still holds -450 for anything that uses it.
abs() hides the sign, so a gain and a loss look the same.

wrong_line_feedback.d: print() shows net faithfully; net itself is wrong.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: He drinks 250 mL more. What is the balance now?
questions.explanation_after_check: intake becomes 1500 + 250 = 1750, so the balance is 1750 − 1050 = +700 mL.
questions.takeaway: So: a name always holds its newest value.
questions.next_bridge: record a flush through his drip.
questions.hint_before_check: The first line changes what intake holds.

code_note.title: Updating a value
code_note.text: A line can replace what a name holds.

science_note.title: A running balance
science_note.text: Fluid charts are running totals: every drink and every output updates the balance through the day.

questions.scene_label: A drink added to the IN pan.

options.feedback: That uses the old intake; the line above updated it.
That is only the new drink, not the balance.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: A 100 mL flush is missing from the balance. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Python treats Intake and intake as two different names. The flush went into a new variable, Intake, so the balance stayed at 700 instead of 800.
questions.takeaway: So: one name, spelled one way.
questions.hint_before_check: Look closely at every letter of each name.

code_note.title: Names
code_note.text: Python is strict about how names are spelled.

science_note.title: Missing volumes
science_note.text: A flush through a drip is real fluid. Charts that drop flushes understate intake, especially in small or elderly patients.

questions.scene_label: The flush lands on its own pan unless the name matches.

b.feedback: == compares and throws the answer away; intake stays 1750.
This works out 1850 but stores it nowhere.

c.feedback: That shows 800, but intake itself is still 1750, so the chart stays wrong elsewhere.
That adds the flush on screen only; intake never stores it.

wrong_line_feedback.c: The print is right; it uses intake, which never changed.

items.title: Oxygen by cannula
items.intro: On nasal cannula, each litre per minute adds about 4% oxygen to the 21% in room air. Let us work out what Mrs Wong is breathing.

recap.title: Oxygen worked out
recap.subtitle: FiO2 from the flow, as a percentage and a fraction, with brackets in the right place.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: At 2 L/min, what FiO2 does Python print?
questions.explanation_after_check: 4 * flow runs first: 4 × 2 = 8, then 21 + 8 = 29%.
questions.takeaway: So: multiply before you add.
questions.next_bridge: turn the percentage into a fraction.

code_note.title: Several operations
code_note.text: When a line has several operations, Python has rules for which comes first.

science_note.title: FiO2
science_note.text: FiO2 is the fraction of oxygen breathed in. Room air is 21%; a nasal cannula adds roughly 4% per litre per minute.

questions.scene_label: A flowmeter set to 2 litres a minute, feeding a nasal cannula.

options.feedback: That adds first: (21 + 4) × 2. Python multiplies first.
That is only the extra oxygen from the flow.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: At 3 L/min, show FiO2 as a fraction
questions.explanation_after_check: 33 / 100 is 0.33: the same oxygen written as a fraction.
questions.takeaway: So: / gives a fraction with decimals.

code_note.title: Dividing
code_note.text: Python has more than one way to divide.

science_note.title: Fractions and percentages
science_note.text: Ventilators and blood gas machines often use FiO2 as a fraction, 0.21 to 1.0, while wards talk in percentages.

questions.scene_label: The flowmeter turned up to 3 litres a minute.

options.feedback: // drops the decimals: 33 // 100 is 0.
% gives the remainder, 33.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: At 4 L/min the code says 100% oxygen. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: The brackets make Python add 21 + 4 first, then multiply by 4: 100%. Only the 4% per litre should be multiplied: 21 + 4 × 4 = 37%.
questions.takeaway: So: bracket only what belongs together.
questions.hint_before_check: Which numbers should the flow multiply?

code_note.title: Brackets
code_note.text: Brackets change which part Python works out first.

science_note.title: Impossible numbers
science_note.text: A nasal cannula cannot deliver 100% oxygen. When code gives a value the device cannot produce, check the formula.

questions.scene_label: The flowmeter at 4 litres a minute.

b.feedback: That multiplies room air by 4: 88%.
That adds the flow to 4 instead of multiplying: 29%.

c.feedback: That forces 37 for this flow only; any other flow comes out wrong.
That shows 1.0, still 100% oxygen.

wrong_line_feedback.c: print() shows fio2 faithfully; fio2 itself is wrong.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: At 5 L/min, what fraction prints?
questions.takeaway: So: work it out, then convert it.
questions.hint_before_check: Work out fio2 first, then divide.

code_note.title: Building on a result
code_note.text: A later line can use a value worked out earlier.

science_note.title: High flows on a cannula
science_note.text: Above about 4 to 6 L/min, cannulas dry the nose and the estimate becomes less reliable; masks are used instead.

questions.scene_label: The flowmeter at 5 litres a minute.

options.feedback: That is the percentage, before dividing by 100.
That is (21 + 4) × 5 / 100, with the multiplication in the wrong place.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The fraction comes out as 21.24. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: / runs before +, so only 4 × 6 = 24 was divided by 100, then 21 added: 21.24. Brackets round the whole sum give 45 / 100 = 0.45.
questions.takeaway: So: to divide a whole sum, bracket it.

code_note.title: What a division covers
code_note.text: Order of operations also decides what a division applies to.

science_note.title: Checking the range
science_note.text: A fraction of oxygen must sit between 0.21 and 1.0. Anything outside that range is a code error, not a patient finding.

questions.scene_label: The flowmeter at 6 litres a minute.

b.feedback: Python already does 4 * flow first; the 21 is still added after dividing: 21.24.
That divides only the flow: still 21.24.

c.feedback: That gives 0.2124, still wrong: the 21 was never divided with the rest.
That rounds 21.24 to 21, still not a fraction.

wrong_line_feedback.c: print() shows frac faithfully; frac itself is wrong.

items.title: Transfusion timing
items.intro: A 350 mL unit of red cells is running at 100 mL an hour. Work out when it will finish, so it ends inside the 4-hour limit.

recap.title: Transfusion timed
recap.subtitle: 3 hours 30 minutes, and a finish time that works past midnight.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many hours will the unit take?
questions.explanation_after_check: 350 / 100 = 3.5 hours; / keeps the half hour.
questions.takeaway: So: / keeps the half hour.
questions.next_bridge: split it into hours and minutes.

code_note.title: Dividing
code_note.text: Python has more than one division symbol.

science_note.title: The 4-hour limit
science_note.text: A unit of red cells should finish within 4 hours of leaving the fridge, to limit the risk of bacterial growth.

questions.scene_label: A unit of red cells hung on a drip stand.

picture.label: Blood bag, level and finish clock

options.feedback: / keeps decimals, so the half hour stays.
That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: How many whole hours is that?
questions.explanation_after_check: minutes is 210, and 210 // 60 is 3 whole hours.
questions.takeaway: So: // gives whole hours.
questions.hint_before_check: Whole hours, with nothing left over.

code_note.title: Whole numbers
code_note.text: Some operators keep only part of a division.

science_note.title: Pump settings
science_note.text: Infusion pumps and handover sheets use hours and minutes, not decimals of an hour.

questions.scene_label: The finish clock, counting whole hours.

picture.label: Blood bag, level and finish clock

options.feedback: / keeps the half: 3.5.
% gives the leftover minutes: 30.
That multiplies: 12600.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many minutes are left over?
questions.explanation_after_check: % gives the remainder: 210 − 3 × 60 = 30 minutes.
questions.takeaway: So: % gives the leftover minutes.
questions.next_bridge: fix the time line in a colleague's script.
questions.hint_before_check: What remains after the whole hours?

code_note.title: Leftovers
code_note.text: Python can give you what is left over after dividing.

science_note.title: Rate and volume
science_note.text: Nurses check the rate against the prescription and the volume against the bag, so both numbers need to be right.

questions.scene_label: The clock, ready for the minutes.

picture.label: Blood bag, level and finish clock

options.feedback: That is the whole hours, from //.
That is half an hour written as a fraction, not minutes.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The script says 3.5 h 30 min. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: / keeps the half hour, so hours is 3.5 and the minutes count it twice. // gives 3 whole hours, and the time reads 3 h 30 min.
questions.takeaway: So: hours with //, minutes with %.

code_note.title: Two kinds of division
code_note.text: The same numbers can divide in different ways.

science_note.title: Handover accuracy
science_note.text: A finish time half an hour out can mean an observation is missed or a unit runs past its limit.

questions.scene_label: A finish time that counts the half hour twice.

picture.label: Blood bag, level and finish clock

b.feedback: round(3.5) gives 4, which adds half an hour that does not exist.
That gives 30, the minutes, as the hours.

c.feedback: That gives 3, the hours, as the minutes.
That gives 3.5 as the minutes.

d.feedback: That hides the decimal on screen, but hours still holds 3.5 for anything else.
That shows 210.0 min, not hours and minutes.

wrong_line_feedback.d: print() shows the two values faithfully.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Started at 22:45, it shows 26:15. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: end is 1575 minutes, which is 26 hours and 15 minutes. % 24 wraps the hours past midnight: 26 % 24 = 2, so it finishes at 2:15.
questions.takeaway: So: % 24 keeps hours on the clock.
questions.hint_before_check: What happens to a clock after 23:59?

code_note.title: Clock times
code_note.text: A 24-hour clock starts again after 23.

science_note.title: Night transfusions
science_note.text: Transfusions that run past midnight need a correct finish time for the night team's checks.

questions.scene_label: A unit started late in the evening.

picture.label: Blood bag, level and finish clock

c.feedback: end % 24 takes a remainder of minutes, not hours: 15.
end // 24 divides minutes by 24: 65.

b.feedback: That only works when the unit passes midnight; a daytime unit would show a negative hour.
That keeps only the minutes: 15.

items.title: GCS total
items.intro: The observation form sends Mr Ali's Glasgow Coma Scale scores as text. Turn them into a total the chart can plot.

recap.title: GCS charted
recap.subtitle: Text turned into numbers, a total of 12, and a drop of 2 flagged.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What does the chart receive?
questions.explanation_after_check: The scores are text, and + joins text: "3" + "4" + "5" makes "345", which is not a GCS at all.
questions.takeaway: Hence, when counting, don't put numbers in quotation marks.

code_note.title: Text and numbers
code_note.text: Quote marks change what `+` does.

science_note.title: The Glasgow Coma Scale
science_note.text: GCS adds eye (1 to 4), verbal (1 to 5) and motor (1 to 6) scores: 15 is fully alert, 3 is the lowest.

questions.scene_label: Mr Ali's eye, verbal and motor scores on the neuro chart.

picture.description: GCS chart with eye, verbal and motor rows and a total marker that slides to the score.
picture.label: GCS chart with a total marker

options.feedback: That would need numbers; these are text in quote marks.

options.label: Error
options.feedback: Joining text with + works; the result is not a sum.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Add the scores as numbers
questions.explanation_after_check: int() turns each text score into a number: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
questions.takeaway: So: convert text to numbers before adding.
questions.next_bridge: fix a script that joins first.
questions.hint_before_check: Turn each text score into a whole number.

code_note.title: Converting text
code_note.text: Python can turn text into other types.

science_note.title: Forms send text
science_note.text: Values typed into forms, apps and spreadsheets usually arrive as text, even when they look like numbers.

questions.scene_label: The chart, waiting for a real total.

picture.description: GCS chart with eye, verbal and motor rows and a total marker that slides to the score.
picture.label: GCS chart with a total marker

options.label: str
options.feedback: str() keeps "3" as text, and text plus a number stops Python with a TypeError.

options.label: float
options.feedback: float() works, but prints 12.0; GCS is a whole number.

options.label: len
options.feedback: len("3") is 1, the number of characters: 1 + 4 + 5 = 10.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The total plots as 345. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: e + v + m joins the text into "345" before int() runs, so int() makes the number 345. Converting each score first gives 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
questions.takeaway: So: convert each score, then add.
questions.hint_before_check: What happens inside the brackets first?

code_note.title: Inside out
code_note.text: Python works out the inside of brackets first.

science_note.title: Impossible scores
science_note.text: A GCS above 15 cannot exist. A chart that accepts one is hiding a code error.

questions.scene_label: A total that plots off the chart.

picture.description: GCS chart with eye, verbal and motor rows and a total marker that slides to the score.
picture.label: GCS chart with a total marker

questions.hint_before_check: Earlier score minus the score now.

code_note.title: Using a stored result
code_note.text: A value worked out earlier can be used again.

science_note.title: A falling GCS
science_note.text: A fall of 2 or more points is a common trigger for urgent medical review.

code_note.text: Not every converter reads every kind of text.

science_note.text: Different systems format the same score differently. Robust code expects that.

items.title: Ward occupancy
items.intro: Ward 7 has 28 beds. Work out what is free and how full it is, for the 8 am bed meeting.

recap.title: Ward board ready
recap.subtitle: Beds free, occupancy to one decimal place, and admissions taken into account.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many beds are free?
questions.explanation_after_check: 28 − 25 = 3 beds free.
questions.takeaway: So: free = total − occupied.
questions.next_bridge: work out how full the ward is.

code_note.title: Subtraction
code_note.text: Order matters when you subtract.

science_note.title: Bed meetings
science_note.text: Hospitals hold daily bed meetings to match free beds with patients waiting in the emergency department.

questions.hint_before_check: Which function keeps a set number of decimals?

code_note.title: Tidying numbers
code_note.text: Python has several built-in functions that change how a number looks or what type it is.

science_note.title: Occupancy targets
science_note.text: Above about 85% occupancy, hospitals struggle to find beds quickly and patients wait longer.

science_note.text: A board that shows empty when the ward is full sends admissions to a ward with no beds.

items.title: Blood group labels
items.intro: Every unit is labelled with its group and Rh sign, like "AB+". Pull the parts out of the label safely.

recap.title: Labels read

questions.ask: What does Python print?
questions.explanation_after_check: Positions start at 0, so bag[0] is the first character, A.
questions.takeaway: So: [0] is the first character.
questions.hint_before_check: Which position does Python count first?

code_note.title: Positions in text
code_note.text: Each character in text has a numbered position.

science_note.title: Labels carry the safety check
science_note.text: Before a transfusion, the group and Rh sign on the bag are checked against the patient, twice.

code_note.title: Counting from the end
code_note.text: Python can count positions from either end.

science_note.title: Rh matters
science_note.text: An Rh-negative patient given Rh-positive blood can make antibodies that complicate later transfusions and pregnancies.
